'''''The Duellists''''' is a 1977 British [[historical drama]] film which is the directorial debut of [[Ridley Scott]]. Set in France during the [[Napoleonic Wars]], the film focuses on a series of duels between two rival officers, the obsessive [[Bonapartism|Bonapartist]] Gabriel Feraud (played by [[Harvey Keitel]]) and [[Monarchism in France|royalist]] Armand d'Hubert ([[Keith Carradine]]), that spans nearly 20 years and reflects the political tumult of early 19th-century France. The film is based on [[Joseph Conrad]]'s 1908 short story "[[The Duel (short story)|The Duel]]".

''The Duellists'' unanimously won the award for Best Debut Film at the [[1977 Cannes Film Festival]], and was nominated for the [[Palme d'Or]].<ref name="Festival-Cannes.com">{{cite web |url=http://www.festival-cannes.com/en/archives/ficheFilm/id/2024/year/1977.html |title=Festival de Cannes: ''The Duellists'' |access-date=10 May 2009 |work=Festival-Cannes.com |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20120927202421/http://www.festival-cannes.com/en/archives/ficheFilm/id/2024/year/1977.html |archive-date=2012-09-27}}</ref> ''The Duellists'' earned widespread acclaim from critics, who praised Scott's direction and visuals, and the film's historical authenticity.<ref name="RT" />{{sfn|Barkman|Barkman|Kang|2013|pp=171–178}} The fight choreography, by master swordsman [[William Hobbs (choreographer)|William Hobbs]], is considered one of the most accurate depictions of dueling in cinema.{{sfn|Barkman|Barkman|Kang|2013|pp=171–178}} At the [[32nd British Academy Film Awards]], the film received nominations for [[BAFTA Award for Best Cinematography|Best Cinematography]] and [[BAFTA Award for Best Costume Design|Best Costume Design]].

==Plot==
=== Strasbourg 1800 ===
[[File:Duell - The Duellists (1978) (18738290228) (cropped).jpg|thumb|The last duel takes place in a ruin, with each combatant armed with two pistols.]]
In [[Strasbourg]] in 1800, Lieutenant Gabriel Feraud of the French [[7th Hussar Regiment (France)|7th Hussars]], a fervent [[Bonapartism|Bonapartist]] and obsessive [[duel]]list, nearly kills the nephew of the city's mayor in a duel. Under pressure from the mayor, Brigadier-General Treillard orders one of his officers, Lieutenant Armand d'Hubert of the [[:Fr:3e régiment de hussards|3rd Hussars]], to place Feraud under house arrest. When D'Hubert delivers the order, Feraud takes it as a personal insult and challenges him to a duel. D'Hubert does all he can to avoid Feraud's unreasonable demand for a duel but is finally left with no honorable way to avoid it. The result is inconclusive, as Feraud gets knocked unconscious before the fight ends. Then d'Hubert is attacked by Feraud's mistress, leaving his face scratched. As a result of the fight, the General dismisses d'Hubert from his staff and returns him to active duty with his regiment.

=== Augsburg 1801 ===
The war interrupts the quarrel and the two do not meet again until six months later. Feraud challenges d'Hubert to another duel and seriously wounds him. While recovering, d'Hubert's lover, Laura, takes care of him and encourages him to end the pointless duels. Instead he takes fencing lessons from a master swordsman, and in the next duel the men fight to a bloody standstill, too tired to hold their swords. They fall to the ground in a wrestle but this is broken apart by the onlookers. Soon afterwards, d'Hubert is relieved to learn he has been promoted to captain, as military discipline forbids officers of different ranks from duelling.

===Lübeck 1806===
By 1806, d'Hubert's unit has been stationed in [[Lübeck]]. He is shocked to hear that the 7th Hussars have arrived in the city and that Feraud is now also a captain. Aware that in two weeks time he is to be promoted to major, d'Hubert attempts to slip away but fails to do it in time. Feraud challenges him to another duel. Before it, d'Hubert happens upon his former lover Laura. She chastises him for continuing to duel Feraud, saying that he will eventually be killed, before bidding him a tearful farewell. In the encounter, which takes place on horseback, d'Hubert slashes Feraud's forehead; with blood flowing into his eyes, Feraud is not capable of continuing the duel. Considering himself the victor, d'Hubert leaves the field ebullient, jumping his horse over a cart. Soon afterwards, Feraud's regiment is posted to Spain while d'Hubert remains stationed in Northern Europe.

===Russia 1812===
The pair (both now colonels) chance upon each other during the French Army's [[retreat from Moscow]], but are forced to cooperate after being separated from the main force. Feraud asks for volunteers to go after Russian [[Cossack]]s and d'Hubert is the only one who will go with him. On foot they are surprised by one of the enemy on horseback, with three others in the distance. Feraud shoots the one closest to them and d'Hubert drives off the others by firing at them. Then d'Hubert jokes "Pistols next time", referring to their next duel and offers Feraud a celebratory drink from his flask, but Feraud silently turns and walks away.

===Tours 1814===
After [[Napoleon#Exile to Elba|Napoleon's exile to Elba]], d'Hubert is now a [[brigadier-general]] recovering from a wartime injury at the home of his sister Leonie in [[Tours]]. She introduces him to Adele, the niece of her neighbour, and the couple fall in love. Colonel Perteley, a Bonapartist agent, attempts to recruit d'Hubert as rumours of Napoleon's imminent [[Hundred Days|return from exile]] abound, but d'Hubert refuses. When Feraud, now a Bonapartist brigadier-general, learns this, he declares he always knew d'Hubert was a traitor.

===Paris 1816===
[[File:Napoleon Bonaparte by Benjamin Robert Haydon.jpg|thumb|upright|Painting of Napoleon in exile on Saint Helena]]

After Napoleon is defeated at [[Battle of Waterloo|Waterloo]], d'Hubert marries Adele and joins the army of [[Louis XVIII]]. Feraud is arrested and is expected to be executed for his part in the [[Hundred Days]] war. Learning of this, d'Hubert calls upon [[Joseph Fouché|the Minister of Police]] and persuades him to spare Feraud. Not knowing d'Hubert saved him, Feraud is paroled to live under [[police supervision]]. Meanwhile, d'Hubert and Adele prepare for the birth of their first child.

===Final Duel 1816===

After learning of d'Hubert's promotion in the new French Army, an incensed Feraud sends two of his former officers to d'Hubert's estate with a challenge for a pistol duel. Reluctantly, d'Hubert agrees. The next day the two men meet in a field near the ruins of a castle. Each man is armed with two single-shot pistols to be fired at will.

After some solitary wandering, the men unknowingly end up within 50 feet of each other. Feraud sees d'Hubert and fires his first shot, missing. D'Hubert plays dead for a moment, coaxing Feraud to fire his second shot, which also misses. D'Hubert's own first shot misses Feraud, but he now has his opponent at point blank range with the only remaining loaded pistol. D'Hubert calmly stands and takes aim while Feraud screams "Go on. Kill me!".

After d'Hubert calmly walks home, he is heard in voiceover telling Feraud that, by all rights and honor, he now owns Feraud's life. D'Hubert tells Feraud that as such, he will simply declare Feraud dead, and that in all future matters concerning the two of them, Feraud shall conduct himself as a dead man and never challenge d'Hubert to another duel or bother his family. D'Hubert returns to his home and pregnant wife to live out the rest of his days in peace. Feraud, on the other hand, returns to his solitary provincial imprisonment, walking disconsolately through the woods, never again to pursue his obsession of dueling.

== Production ==
===Development===
''The Duellists'' would mark the feature film debut of Ridley Scott, who had previously made television commercials.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ridley-Scott|title=Ridley Scott: British director and producer|website=Encyclopædia Britannica|access-date=26 October 2020}}</ref> Its visual style was influenced by [[Stanley Kubrick]]'s [[historical drama]] ''[[Barry Lyndon]]'' (1975).<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.filmlinc.org/films/the-duellists/|title= The Duellists: Ridley Scott|website=filmlinc.org|date=26 October 2020}}</ref> In both films, duels play an essential role. In his commentary for the DVD release of the film, Scott comments that he was trying to emulate the lush cinematography of Kubrick's film, which approached the naturalistic paintings of the era depicted.

Due to budgetary constraints, Scott decided to shoot the film in a series of [[Scene (drama)|tableaux]] to indicate chapters of the story.{{sfn|Parrill|2011|loc=[https://books.google.com/books?id=UyAsYDcQkjIC&dq=Vaughan-Hughes+the+duellist+screenplay&pg=PA35 35]}} The film was made with advice from military historian [[Richard Holmes (military historian)|Richard Holmes]].

===Writing===
[[File:Général FRANCOIS FOURNIER SARLOVEZE.jpg|thumb|200px|[[François Fournier-Sarlovèze]], the basis for Feraud]]
Scott initially hired Gerald Vaughan-Hughes to write a story about [[Guy Fawkes]] and the 1605 [[Gunpowder Plot]], but when financing fell through,{{sfn|Parrill|2011|p=30}} Vaughan-Hughes adapted the screenplay from the 1907 [[novella]] ''The Duel'' by British-Polish writer [[Joseph Conrad]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Gerald Vaughan-Hughes |url=https://www2.bfi.org.uk/films-tv-people/4ce2ba28922af |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190305192520/http://www.bfi.org.uk/films-tv-people/4ce2ba28922af |url-status=dead |archive-date=5 March 2019 |access-date=26 October 2020 |website=BFI}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/41635636|title=Youthful Resentment, Bourgeois (Anti-)Heroism and Sublime Unrest: Conrad's 'The Duel' and Ridley Scott's "The Duellists"|first=Flavio |last=Gregori|journal=South Atlantic Review|volume=75|number=3|date=Summer 2010|pages=109–129|jstor=41635636}}</ref> The genesis of Conrad's story were the real duels during the Napoleonic era between two officers in France's ''[[Grande Armée]]'', [[Pierre Dupont de l'Étang]] and [[François Fournier-Sarlovèze]], who became D’Hubert and Feraud in ''The Duel''.<ref name="fence">{{cite web|url=https://historicalfencer.com/the-real-men-behind-the-duellist/|date=28 September 2018|title=The real men behind The Duellists|first=Anders |last=Linnard |website=historicalfencer.com}}</ref> In ''The Encyclopedia of the Sword'', Nick Evangelista wrote:
{{Blockquote | As a young officer in Napoleon's Army, Dupont [l'Étang] was ordered to deliver a disagreeable message to a fellow officer, Fournier [Fournier-Sarlovèze], a rabid duellist. Fournier, taking out his subsequent rage on the messenger, challenged Dupont to a duel. This sparked a succession of encounters, waged with sword and pistol, that spanned decades. The contest was eventually resolved when Dupont was able to overcome Fournier in a pistol duel, forcing him to promise never to bother him again.<ref>{{cite book|last1= Evangelista |first1= Nick|title=The Encyclopedia of the Sword|date=1995|publisher= Greenwood Press |location= Westport, [[Connecticut|CT]] |isbn=0-313-27896-2|page= 187 |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=TyJ8ebnS1HMC&pg=PA187}}</ref>}}

The pair fought their first duel in 1794 from which Fournier-Sarlovèze – known as the "worst subject of the ''Grande Armée''"<ref name="fence"/> – demanded a rematch. At least another 30 rematches then occurred over the next 19 years in which the two officers fought mounted and on foot with swords, sabres, and pistols. After l'Étang finally bested Fournier-Sarlovèze in a duel, he told him to leave him alone for good. Fournier-Sarlovèze died aged 53; l'Étang lived until he was 74.<ref name="fence"/>

Although Vaughan-Hughes' screenplay used many elements from ''The Duel'', it created new scenes like the duels at the start and the end of the film and new characters.{{sfn|Parrill|2011|pp=32–34}} It also moved the date of the first duel from 1794 to 1800. [[Alex von Tunzelmann]] speculates that this was an attempt to mirror Napoleon's life.<ref name="von-Tunzelmann-2010"/>

=== Casting ===
Scott's first choices to play the lead roles were [[Oliver Reed]] and [[Michael York]], the stars of [[The Three Musketeers (1973 live-action film)|''The Three Musketeers'']], but they proved unavailable or out of the film's budget range. [[Paramount Pictures]] gave Scott a list of four actors from which to choose for the two leads, which he had to agree to in order to receive financing. Scott selected [[Keith Carradine]] and [[Harvey Keitel]], then spent several months trying to convince them to accept the roles. Carradine and Keitel, both Americans, chose not to adapt accents to match their British co-stars, believing their natural idiolects better reflected their character's class and ideological backgrounds. The leads insisted upon using real, un-dulled 1798-pattern light cavalry saber swords for the sword dueling sequences.

Even though he was out of the film's budget, [[Albert Finney]] agreed to appear in the film at the behest of this then-girlfriend [[Diana Quick]]. He filmed his scene in a single day, and took a case of [[champagne]] as payment.

===Filming===
Many exteriors were shot in and around [[Sarlat-la-Canéda]] in the [[Dordogne]] region of France. The winter scenes set during the retreat from Moscow were shot in the [[Cairngorms]] of [[Scotland]], near [[Aviemore]]. The final duel scene was filmed at the unrestored [[Château de Commarque]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.movie-locations.com/movies/d/Duellists.html#.WpTNgGbMwkp|title= Worldwide Guide to Movie Locations|website=movie-locations.com|access-date=26 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130302150130/http://www.movie-locations.com/movies/d/Duellists.html |archive-date=2013-03-02}}</ref>

The last scene references paintings of the former emperor in his South Atlantic exile (e.g. ''Napoleon on Saint Helena'' by Franz Josef Sandmann).{{sfn|Barkman|Barkman|Kang|2013|loc=[https://books.google.com/books?id=jdJPucpdi4MC&dq=Napoleon+on+Saint+Helena++ridley+scott&pg=PA49 49]}}

==Critical reception==
The film holds a 75% rating on [[Rotten Tomatoes]] based on 63 reviews, with an average score of 7.5/10 and the critical consensus: "Rich, stylized visuals work with effective performances in Ridley Scott's take on Joseph Conrad's Napoleonic story, resulting in an impressive feature film debut for the director."<ref name="RT">{{cite web |url= http://www.rottentomatoes.com/m/duellists |title= ''The Duellists'' (1977) |access-date= 7 May 2026 |publisher= Rotten Tomatoes }}</ref> [[Metacritic]], which uses a [[Weighted arithmetic mean|weighted average]], assigned the film a score of 70 out of 100, based on 13 critics, indicating "generally favorable" reviews.<ref name="Metacritic">{{cite web |title=''The Duellists'' |url=https://www.metacritic.com/movie/the-duellists |website=[[Metacritic]] |publisher=[[Fandom (website)#Fandom, Inc.|Fandom, Inc.]] |access-date=21 October 2025 |archive-url= |archive-date= |url-status=}}</ref>

[[Vincent Canby]] of ''[[The New York Times]]'' wrote: "The movie, set during the Napoleonic Wars, uses its beauty much in the way that other movies use soundtrack music, to set mood, to complement scenes and even to contradict them.  Sometimes it's all too much, yet the camerawork, which is by Frank Tidy, provides the Baroque style by which the movie operates on our senses, making the eccentric drama at first compelling and ultimately breathtaking."<ref>{{Cite news |last=Canby |first=Vincent |author-link=Vincent Canby |date=14 January 1978 |title=New Movie, 'The Duellists,' Is Set During Napoleonic Wars |page=10 |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref> [[Pauline Kael]] of ''[[The New Yorker]]'' wrote, "''The Duellists'' is an epic yarn; we sit back and observe it, and it's consistently entertaining—and eerily beautiful."<ref>{{Cite news |last=Kael |first=Pauline |date=23 January 1978 |title=The Current Cinema |page=80 |work=[[The New Yorker]]}}</ref> [[Gene Siskel]] of the ''[[Chicago Tribune]]'' gave the film two-and-a-half stars out of four and wrote, "The story might have worked if there were an undercurrent of attractiveness to Keitel's loutish character. But he is an unwavering boor from start to finish, and his prowess with weapons is in no way redeeming."<ref>{{Cite news |last=Siskel |first=Gene |author-link=Gene Siskel |date=2 April 1979 |title='The Duellists': Pretty, but plot is a lost cause |work=[[Chicago Tribune]]}}</ref> ''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'' wrote that Ridley Scott "does have an eye for fine compositions, period recreation and arresting tableaus. But it is somewhat surface and too taken up with poses… it rarely illuminates the deeper human aspects of these two flailing men."<ref>{{Cite news |date=1 June 1977 |title=Film Reviews: The Duellists |page=17 |work=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]}}</ref>

[[Charles Champlin]] of the ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'' wrote that the sword fights were "the best I've ever seen" and called the story "refreshingly different from standard film content."<ref>{{Cite news |last=Champlin |first=Charles |date=27 January 1978 |title=Taste of Steel in 'Duellists' |work=[[Los Angeles Times]]}}</ref> Michael Webb of ''[[The Washington Post]]'' wrote, "The film has the pictorial beauty and rich period sense of ''[[Barry Lyndon]]'' (1975), but adds the narrative drive and passion that Kubrick's film lacked."<ref>{{Cite news |last=Webb |first=Michael |date=3 June 1977 |title=Cannes Festival: A Case of Expecting the Worst—and Getting It |page=B4 |work=[[The Washington Post]]}}</ref> [[David Ansen]] of ''[[Newsweek]]'' wrote, "The best you can say about the film – the directing debut of Ridley Scott – is that it provides an unusually civilized experience in these days of movie barbarism…  The worst that can be said is that Keitel and Carradine are so perversely cast as French hussars that, whenever they speak, the splendid illusion of nineteenth-century Europe is shattered."<ref>{{cite news|last=Ansen |first=David |date=30 January 1978 |title=Misfire |work=[[Newsweek]] |page=55}}</ref>

The film is lauded for its historically authentic portrayal of Napoleonic uniforms and military conduct, as well as its generally accurate early-19th-century fencing techniques as recreated by fight choreographer [[William Hobbs (choreographer)|William Hobbs]].{{sfn|Barkman|Barkman|Kang|2013|pp=171–178}}<ref name="von-Tunzelmann-2010">{{cite news |title= The Duellists: it takes two to tangle |url= https://www.theguardian.com/film/2010/oct/28/the-duellists-reel-history | work = The Guardian|date=10 January 2016}}</ref>

The film is included in the second edition of ''The New York Times Guide to the Best 1,000 Movies Ever Made'', published in 2004.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/ref/movies/1000best.html |title=The Best 1,000 Movies Ever Made |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=29 April 2003 |access-date=12 June 2008 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20080612032429/https://www.nytimes.com/ref/movies/1000best.html |archive-date=2008-06-12}}</ref>

[[Gregory Widen]] stated ''The Duellists'' was the inspiration for him to write ''[[Highlander (film)|Highlander]]''.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Power |first=Ed |date=June 16, 2016 |title=There can be only one: why Highlander will live forever |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/films/2016/06/16/there-can-only-be-one-why-highlander-will-live-forever/ |access-date=2026-01-02 |work=The Telegraph |language=en-GB |issn=0307-1235}}</ref>{{Better source needed|reason=Widen’s comments in this source only suggest that the idea of Highlander is a riff on The Duellists; he didn't confirm The Duellists as the inspiration.|date=January 2026}}

== Novelization ==
A novelization of the film by [[Gordon Williams (writer)|Gordon Williams]], which included historical contexts and slightly expanded the plot, was published by [[HarperCollins|Fontana Books]] in Great Britain in 1977<ref>{{cite book |last1=Williams |first1=Gordon |title=The Duellists |year=1977 |publisher=Fontana Books |location=Great Britain |isbn=978-0006150572}}</ref> and by [[Pocket Books]] ({{ISBN|0-671-81930-5}}) in the United States in 1978.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Williams |first1=Gordon |title=The Duellists |year=1978 |publisher=Pocket Books |location=New York |isbn=978-0671819309}}</ref>

==Home media==
On 29 January 2013, [[Shout! Factory]] released the film on [[Blu-ray]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.blu-ray.com/movies/The-Duellists-Blu-ray/52668 |title=''The Duellists'' Blu-ray |website=Blu-ray.com. |access-date= 5 February 2014}}</ref> The release coincided with the publication of an essay on the film in a collection of scholarly essays on Ridley Scott.{{sfn|Mahon|2013|loc=[https://www.academia.edu/12374141/Honor_in_The_Duellists 45-60]}}
